source.title: J-Anchor: Defending Against Prefill Attacks via J-Space Selective Refusal Restoration

record.file_problem: No apparent file problem; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests a single difference-in-means refusal direction through a selective hidden-state restoration variant and measures harmful-request outcomes, but it does not use the original ablation procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper's main J-Anchor results use a multi-axis J-lens refusal subspace, not the difference-in-means direction. Those results are not rows for V1. Table 3's hidden-state refusal variant uses a single direction formed from harmful-versus-benign mean hidden states and reports attack success. The paper also describes refusal and harmfulness signal trajectories; it does not give their numerical values in the text.
record.test_reason: This is a prefill-jailbreak defense paper, a new setting for the claim. It tests the claim in two places. First, an ablation variant and a baseline add a difference-in-means (harmful minus benign) refusal direction and report the resulting refusal (attack success rate, over-refusal) under fixed and deep prefill attacks. Second, it reports that the refusal signal erodes while the harmfulness signal persists, which bears on V5. Its main method uses a J-lens vocabulary subspace, not the difference-in-means direction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that prefill attacks erode refusal faster than harmfulness recognition (refusal-state erosion). They find that J-Anchor, which selectively restores the pre-attack refusal state in a J-lens refusal subspace, sharply cuts attack success while largely preserving benign behavior and reasoning. Their ablations favor the J-lens subspace over random, logit-lens and hidden-state (difference-in-means) variants.
record.recipe_differences: The tested single-direction variant forms a harmful-minus-benign hidden-state mean direction at the assistant role token and selectively restores it using an anchor and gate. It does not project the direction out or test unconditional addition. The paper's main J-Anchor method instead uses a multi-axis J-lens refusal subspace.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model and prefill depth; the hidden-state variant leaves higher residual ASR on Qwen3-8B under deep prefill. Random-direction restoration is similarly effective on Gemma-4-E4B-IT.

fits_no_version.finding: Under prefill attacks, the J-lens vocabulary-grounded refusal subspace score erodes over prefill tokens. Restoring it (J-Anchor) lowers ASR to ≤3.8% fixed and ≤11.5% deep prefill.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prefill jailbreaks act by eroding a refusal representation (read in J-space) rather than harm recognition; this is close to V3 but uses a different direction or subspace.

record.problems: The hidden-state direction variant is selectively restored rather than ablated or added unconditionally. The study does not report harmless-request or reasoning outcomes for that variant. The main text provides no uncertainty estimates for the reported ASRs, and the signal-trajectory description gives no numerical values. Random-direction controls also achieve very low ASR on Gemma-4-E4B-IT.

untested.parts: Directional ablation removing refusal; unconditional addition on harmless prompts with the hidden-state variant; capability retention for that variant.
All. The study uses an abliterated Gemma-3-27B only to generate deep prefills and does not evaluate it.
Whether attacks suppress the difference-in-means direction specifically; adversarial training against ablation.
All. The main method uses a multi-axis J-lens refusal subspace, but the study does not compare it with a single direction as a description of refusal.
All. Thinking mode is disabled on the Qwen models.

missing.what: Refusal Vector baseline (Arditi difference-in-means direction added at α=0.5): StrongREJECT ASR under fixed prefill. Llama 65.2→42.8; Gemma 82.7→85.6; Qwen3.5 77.3→82.8; Qwen3-8B 67.7→5.8.
Refusal Vector baseline under deep prefill (StrongREJECT). Llama 90.4→87.5; Gemma 92.3→93.9; Qwen3.5 91.7→91.1; Qwen3-8B 90.7→67.7.
Refusal Vector induces over-refusal on benign prompts (XSTest ORR). Llama 7.6→60.8; Gemma 12.0→80.0; Qwen3.5 6.0→27.6; Qwen3-8B 4.0→32.8. OKTest rises similarly.
Refusal Vector causes the largest reasoning accuracy drops on GSM8K/MATH500 (figure only); judge-based accuracies are in Table 6.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence on V1 is indirect. It comes from a defense ablation and a baseline under prefill attacks. The hidden-state variant's parameters were tuned on test-benchmark ASR. No uncertainty is reported. The dataset of record should add the Refusal Vector baseline rows, which show the original direction's added form inducing benign over-refusal but failing to restore refusal under prefill in three of four models.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the direction, add it as an unconditional intervention, test it across every layer and position, measure induced refusal on harmless requests for this variant, or report this variant's general-capability outcomes.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the original single direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not test whether refusal is best described as affine, a cone, or a dominant direction plus other directions.

Measures vocabulary-grounded harmfulness and refusal signals during prefill and generation, but does not establish that these are distinct causal representations of a harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No transfer test across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
No comparison of refusal-training procedures or training stages.
No test of the claim in reasoning models; Qwen3-family thinking mode is disabled.

The two arms are not matched: random directions use J-Anchor's J-lens gate, while the variant uses its own hidden-state gate and separately tuned ρ and τ. The record's verdict for this condition is limits_scope, but the synthesis files it under challenges.

statements.correction: Gemma-4-E4B-IT, StrongREJECT. Hidden-state difference-in-means gated restoration: 82.7%→0.0% (fixed), 92.3%→1.6% (deep). Arditi Refusal Vector (official pipeline, one layer, α=0.5 because α=1 over-refused, unconditional): 82.7%→85.6% (fixed), 92.3%→93.9% (deep). The two directions are built differently.
statements.problem: Under fixed prefill, gated restoration reaches 0.0%, not 1.6% (1.6% is the deep-prefill cell). It is also not the same Arditi vector. The hidden-state variant uses its own difference-in-means direction from AdvBench-dev420 vs 500 WildJailbreak benign prompts at the assistant role token, applied at all layers between 40% and 85% of depth. The Refusal Vector baseline uses the direction from Arditi's official pipeline at one selected layer. On Gemma, random directions with a gate also reach 0.3%, so the contrast may reflect the gate rather than the direction.

statements.correction: This study is arXiv:2611.01342 (31 Oct 2026). Under prefill attacks, both the J-lens harmfulness and refusal signals weaken. Refusal falls to or near the benign baseline (z=0). Harmfulness stays above the benign baseline during generation. Failed attacks show stronger refusal recovery. The text gives no numbers, model or n. The finding is correlational.
statements.problem: The statement gives no numbers for this study, and its text is cut off.
